Chapter 23
How Flatterers Should Be Avoided

I must not skip over a critical topic. Princes constantly face a specific danger, and they will only survive it if they are highly careful and sharp. I am talking about flatterers. Courts are completely full of them. People are naturally so pleased with themselves and so easily blind to their own flaws that it is incredibly hard to escape this pest. But when a ruler tries to defend himself against flattery, he risks losing the respect of his people. The only true way to protect yourself from flatterers is to make men understand that telling you the truth will not offend you. However, if absolutely anyone is allowed to tell you the truth, you will quickly lose their respect.

Therefore, a wise prince must take a third approach. He should choose the wise men in his state and give only them the freedom to tell him the truth. Even then, they should only speak about the things he specifically asks about, and absolutely nothing else. However, he should question these advisors on everything. He must listen to their opinions and then form his own conclusions independently. When dealing with his council, both individually and as a group, the prince must act so that every advisor knows this: the more freely they speak, the more the prince will favor them. Outside of this select group, he should refuse to listen to anyone. Once he makes a decision, he must follow it through relentlessly and stand firm in his choices. A ruler who does anything else will either be destroyed by flatterers or constantly change his mind based on conflicting advice. Either way, he will lose all respect.

Let me offer a modern example. Fra Luca, an agent for Maximilian the First, the present emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, once spoke about his majesty. Maximilian, born in 1459, became deeply involved in Italian politics through his marriages to Mary, daughter of Charles the Bold, and later to Bianca Sforza. Fra Luca said that the emperor consulted with absolutely no one, yet he never got his way in anything. This happened because Maximilian followed a practice completely opposite to the rules I just laid out. The emperor is a highly secretive man. He never shares his plans with anyone, and he refuses to listen to any opinions. But as soon as he tries to put his plans into action, they are revealed to the public. Instantly, the men around him start pushing back and obstructing his efforts. Because the emperor is weak and easily swayed, he changes his mind. As a result, whatever he does one day, he undoes the very next day. No one ever understands what he actually wants or intends to do, and absolutely no one can rely on his decisions.

A prince must always seek advice, but only when he wants it, not when others want to give it. In fact, he should strongly discourage anyone from offering opinions unless he specifically asks for them. However, he needs to constantly ask questions. After asking, he must listen patiently to the answers. Furthermore, if he ever discovers that someone held back the truth for any reason, the prince must unleash his anger and make them regret it.

Some people believe that if a prince appears wise, it is not due to his own natural ability, but simply because he has good advisors around him. These people are completely wrong. This is an unbreakable rule: a prince who is not wise on his own will never be able to take good advice. The only exception is if he accidentally hands total control over to one incredibly smart man. In that rare case, his state might run well, but it will not last long. That clever governor will quickly overthrow the prince and steal his power.

On the other hand, if an inexperienced prince tries to take advice from multiple advisors, he will never get unified answers. He will also have no idea how to bring their conflicting opinions together. Every single advisor will selfishly focus on his own personal interests. The prince will not know how to control them or see through their hidden agendas. You cannot expect anything better, because men will always betray you unless they are forced to be honest. Therefore, the conclusion is clear: good advice, no matter where it comes from, only exists because the prince is wise. A prince does not become wise simply by getting good advice.
